title: Moving the spotlight
goal: Use verbs that focus on the object, the receiver and the thing moved — the part of Tagalog that feels most foreign to English speakers, and the part that matters most.
bekal: seeing that *ang* marks a specific, known thing, not the doer
building *-in*, *i-* and *-an* verbs in three aspects
choosing the right focus for what you want to highlight

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sino ang kumain ng tinapay?
dialogs.intro: Morning. The bread Ana left on the table is gone, and the investigation begins.

notes: **Kumain and kinain share the same root.** The difference isn't time but **who is in the spotlight**. *Kumain ang bata ng tinapay* spotlights the child; *Kinain ng bata ang tinapay* spotlights the bread. Both mean "the child ate bread" — and both are correct.

**One rule explains the whole system:** whatever is marked with *ang* is in the spotlight, and **the verb form must match that spotlight**. Spotlight on the doer: *mag-/-um-/ma-*. On the object: *-in*. On the receiver: *-an*. On the thing being moved: *i-*.

**When to use object focus?** A rule of thumb that rarely fails: **if the thing is specific — that one, the one we know — use object focus.** Ana's bread is specific bread, so *kinain*. If you eat just any bread: *kumain ako ng tinapay*.

**The doer moves to ng.** Look at *kinain **ko***, *ibibigay **ko***, *binigyan **ninyo***. Once the spotlight moves to the object, the doer is demoted and takes the *ng* set. This is why Tagalog sentences can sound "passive" to English ears — but it isn't passive, it's focus.
**Bilhan mo ako ng gatas** uses receiver focus: the spotlight is on **me**, the person being bought for. Compare *bumili ako ng gatas* (I bought milk) and *binili ko ang gatas* (I bought the milk).
**Ibibigay ko sa iyo** focuses on the thing being moved. *I-* verbs almost always deal with something changing hands or place: *ibigay* (give), *ilagay* (put), *itapon* (throw away), *isara* (close).

**Everyday commands are almost always object focus.** *Kainin mo!* (eat it), *Isara mo ang pinto* (close the door), *Basahin mo ito* (read this). If you want to sound natural when asking someone to do something, this is the form to master.
**Akala ko** = "I thought". Always used for a guess that turned out wrong, so it nearly always comes with an apology — like English "I thought it was…".
**Ako na ang bibili** uses the emphasis pattern *X ang Y*: "let me be the one who buys". The most common way to volunteer, and *na* here means "never mind, let me".

grammars.title: Four focuses, one event
body: One and the same event — someone buying bread for a friend — can be told from four angles. The meaning doesn't change; what changes is who stands in the spotlight.

head: Focus
Sentence
In the spotlight
Translation
rows: **Bumili** ako ng tinapay para kay Ana.
The bread, I gave to Ana.

after: Notice that **the doer is always the same** — me. What changes is the marker: *ako* (the *ang* set) when the doer is in the spotlight, *ko* (the *ng* set) when it isn't.
English does something similar with active and passive: "I bought the bread" versus "the bread was bought by me". The difference: Tagalog has four angles, not two, and uses them far more often.
At A1, master the first two, and be able to **recognize** the last two when you hear them.

grammars.title: Building object-focus verbs
body: All three affixes use the infix **-in-** to show the action has started, and syllable repetition to show it isn't finished — the same pattern as units 11 and 12.
after: Roots starting with a vowel take the prefix *in-* instead of the infix: *inom* → *ininom*, *abot* → *inabot*.
Some roots change shape slightly with *-in* or *-an*: *bili* → *bilhin*, *dala* → *dalhin*, *bigay* → *bigyan*, *kuha* → *kunin*. A small group to learn as they are.

⚠️ Don't panic at this table. In everyday conversation, what you'll need most is the **command** form (*kainin mo*, *isara mo*, *bigyan mo*) and the **done** form (*kinain*, *binili*, *ibinigay*). The rest will come on its own.

blocks.text: This is where object focus shows up most in real life. Notice that the doer is *mo* or *ninyo*, not *ka*.
Adding *po* and the prefix *paki-* turns all of these into polite requests: *Pakisara po ng pinto.* Use this form with older people or strangers — a bare command sounds rude in any language.

blocks.title: Telling someone not to
items: *Huwag* + pronoun + verb: *Huwag kang umalis* (don't go), *Huwag mong kainin* (don't eat it).
Notice the linker that appears: *huwag **kang***, *huwag **mong***. This is the *-ng* linker you've known since unit 3.

blocks.text: This question haunts every learner of Tagalog. The table below is the most practical summary possible.

head: If you want to…
Use focus
Example
rows: talk about a specific thing (that one)
say who the action is for

blocks.text: If it all feels like too much at once, hold on to this one sentence: **a specific thing calls for object focus.** English marks this with "the" versus "a"; in Tagalog, the marker is the verb form itself.

blocks.title: Mistakes that are okay
items: Using doer focus where object focus belongs **won't cause misunderstandings**. People will understand *Kumain ako ng tinapay mo* — a bit odd, but clear.
So don't wait until you've mastered it all before you start speaking. Focus improves fastest through listening, and slowest through memorizing tables.

exercises.prompt: Change from doer focus to object focus. Example: Kumain ako ng tinapay. → Kinain ko ang tinapay.

items: I'll give it to you later.
